RIME MINISTER Narendra Modi’s successful visit to
Ethiopia illustrates India’s approach towards Africa,
rooted in personal diplomacy, historical ties, and stra-
tegicre-engagement. Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed per-
sonally welcomed Modi, drove him to engagements,
and saw him off. This “car diplomacy” underscores the impor-
tance he places on direct personal communication.
Although Modi did not formaily visit the African UnionCom-
mission, his meeting with AU Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Yous-
soufat the state banquet was significant. With the Fourth India-
Africa Forum Summit on the horizon, this interactionisexpected
to generate positive institutional follow-up.

Africa Forum Summit on thehorizon, thisinteractionisexpecter

Emerging from years ofcivil war and navigating regional ten-
sions across the Horn of Africa, involving Sudan, Somalia, and
Egypt, Ethiopia has been diplomatically constrained. Modi’sar-
rival, the first visit by amajor BRICS head, helped Ethiopiasignal
its return to international engagement. Indiaearlier played akey
rolein supporting Ethiopia’s successful bid to join BRICS .
Amajor outcome of the visit wasthe elevation ofbilateral ties
to astrategic partnership, reflecting cooperation acrosseconomic,
educational, development, and security domains. As Ethiopia
pursuesaccesstothe Red Sea, whether through partsofSomalia
or via arrangements with Eritrea, moves that carry inherent risks
of regional destabilisation and require caution, India’s role as a
trusted strategic partner can help temper these ambitions.
Ethiopia also benefited from India’s defence training and ca-
pacity-building initiatives. After years of military engagement,
its armed forces require replenishment in equipment and capa-
bility. Adefence partnership would allow Ethiopia to diversify.
Indianeducation hasimmense respect in Ethiopia. The deci-
sion to double ICCR scholarships, utilise ITEC fellowships, and
extend AI-foctised training under ITEC reflects this legacy. Ethio-
pia sends many PhD students to India under its programmes.
Given its population of over 130 million, Ethiopia should be en-
couraged to establish Indian-supported institutions locally.
Onegap was the absenceofa business engagement. Ethiopia

Across India, caste, class and religious orthodoxies continue
to police intimacy, with inter-faith and inter-caste couples fre-
quently facing hostility, coercion and violence from families and
communities, often withnohelp from institutions meant tosafe-
guard their freedoms. From Lata Singh (2006) to S Khushboo

against this moral vigilantism, affirming the right of consenting
adults tochoose their partners without intervention from society
or state. Read in this light, the Allahabad HC’s intervention is a
modest but necessary corrective—anassertion that the law must
recognise adults as rights-bearing citizens, not wardsto be steered
towardssocially approved choices.
